notes.claim: A teacher describes the "chuck it on the other side and it changes sign" shortcut as working for a great number of equations.
notes.contested: Bitesize National 5 teaches the shortcut "change side, change operation" as the general rule, while a teacher says it works for a great number of equations but prefers the balance method, which other Bitesize pages use.

notes.claim: BBC Bitesize National 5 (Scotland) teaches the general rule "change side, change operation" for changing the subject.
A formula remains balanced if the same operation is performed on both sides.
SQA lists the ability to transpose engineering formulae as advantageous on entry to its HN Engineering Mathematics 1 unit.
Bitesize says to start with the last operation and work back to the first.

sources.title: 2.11 Rearranging formulas 2
sources.quote: A formula remains balanced if we perform the same operation to both sides of it.

sources.title: Changing the subject of a formula - KS3 Maths - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: Start with the last operation and work back to the first.

sources.title: Article - Misconceptions: Solving Equations - Mr Barton Maths Podcast
sources.quote: The problem is, of course, that the change side, change sign method works absolutely perfectly for a great number of equations.

sources.title: Changing the subject of a formula - Changing the subject of a formula - National 5 Maths Revision - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: To change the subject of a formula the terms are rearranged following the general rule, change side, change operation.

sources.title: national unit specification: general information
sources.quote: it would be advantageous if learners had good algebraic skills together with an ability to transpose engineering formulae and solve simple trigonometric equations.
